transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-27 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Nina Alvarez (Redwood CSM), Carlos Mendoza (Peregrine Head of ML), Priya Singh (Product), Liam O'Connor (SRE), Sofia Reyes (Data Eng)
---
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, really quick intro — i'm maya redwood, ethan is our se, nina cs, and we wanted to kick off the poc scoping for the routing assistant project. carlos, want to kick us off with the top goals?
[00:22] Carlos Mendoza: yeah sure, um main goal is to reduce manual re-routing and exceptions in our last-mile flows, so we want to validate two things: one, accuracy/quality of the model on our domain prompts, and two, that it can handle our peak load without blowing cost targets.
[00:38] Priya Singh: timeline is roughly q1 sprint to prove viability — we have execs wanting a go/no-go in ~6 weeks.
[00:50] Ethan Park: great — that aligns with a typical redwood pilot. Quick clarifying q: when you say accuracy what metrics do you care about? exact match? pass/fail? human rating?
[01:05] Carlos Mendoza: good question. we want a blended score: human acceptability (binary pass/fail per case), plus a precision-like metric for entity extraction and slot-filling. also hallucination rate — false but plausible actions are a showstopper.
[01:22] Maya Chen: perfect — for POC we usually propose a golden set + regression set approach: golden set ~200 high-value examples annotated by the customer for pass/fail, regression ~1k to spot distributional errors. is that feasible for you?
[01:36] Sofia Reyes: 200 golden prompts is doable; we can pull from production logs and add manual annotations. i'll need a template for the expected format.
[01:45] Ethan Park: we'll share a CSV template (prompt, expected answer, tolerance flags, format regex) and example labeling guidelines. note: some transcriptions may show K V cache as K V cash in older docs so we'll be explicit about KV cache naming.
[02:05] Liam O'Connor: on the infra side our SREs want to know if this will be hosted or dedicated. what's the tradeoff on latency/cost?
[02:16] Maya Chen: hosted is fastest to stand up — lower lead time, pay-as-you-go. dedicated gives you reserved capacity and tighter latency SLOs. for something with consistent traffic at peak, dedicated usually gives better per-token economics.
[02:30] Carlos Mendoza: our 95th percentile latency target is 400ms for decision path generation, and peak concurrent requests hit about 120 QPS during shift changes. average token length is around 180 tokens per request.
[02:44] Ethan Park: ok that's super helpful. with 120 qps and 180 tokens avg we should plan for batching behavior; we'll show how continuous batching and prefix caching reduces token compute. we'll also propose a quantization profile for cost savings.
[03:02] Priya Singh: what about hallucination checks? we need deterministic format and no invented locations or carrier names.
[03:10] Ethan Park: we recommend two checks: syntactic format validation (regex/JSON schema) and semantic hallucination detection. semantically we run a scoring step that flags answers with hallucination heuristics — e.g., external-entity invention, confident but unsupported routing steps.
[03:28] Carlos Mendoza: how do you score those heuristics?
[03:30] Ethan Park: we use a weighted scoring system for the POC: 50% human acceptability on golden-set, 20% hallucination rate (lower is better), 15% format-compliance, 15% latency/cost bucket. those weights are negotiable.
[03:48] Maya Chen: to expand, acceptance gates would be: >=85% pass rate on golden set, hallucinations <3% on regression set, format compliance >=98% on golden. latency within 95th < 400ms or we discuss Dedicated config.
[04:05] Priya Singh: acceptable. any recommended golden prompt composition? types?
[04:12] Ethan Park: yes, split golden set across categories: 40% typical routing, 30% edge cases (exceptions), 20% long-context chaining prompts, 10% adversarial/hallucination-targeted. include expected outputs and tolerance.
[04:31] Carlos Mendoza: good. on regression set, do you have guidance on size and sampling?
[04:35] Ethan Park: 1k is the typical minimum for signal on distributional regressions; we prefer randomized sampling from production logs (stratified by route type and token length).
[04:49] Sofia Reyes: we'll need to sanitize PII. can we do local masking before sending?
[04:56] Maya Chen: yes, sanitize first. we also support redwood private for on-prem runs, but for POC many customers prefer sanitized sample in hosted env. we'll share data handling and our KMS integration notes.
[05:12] Liam O'Connor: security checklist — SSO, SAML, log retention, audit logs. we need SOC2 and key mgmt info.
[05:20] Nina Alvarez: i'll attach SOC2 and a short security doc after the meeting. we also have a compliance page and can do an NDA redline if needed.
[05:30] Carlos Mendoza: cost sensitivity — execs want a cost estimate for projected monthly run at production load if this goes to prod.
[05:37] Maya Chen: we'll include cost modeling in the SOW: sample runs at your token distribution, delta between hosted and dedicated, and expected op ex.
[05:45] Priya Singh: for the benchmark run itself what do we need to provide?
[05:50] Ethan Park: three things: 1) golden set CSV, 2) regression corpus (1k), 3) a traffic profile (qps per hour, token distribution, concurrency). we'll run bench for 1-2 hour windows to capture warm cache and steady-state.
[06:12] Carlos Mendoza: warm cache — how much impact do you see from prefix caching?
[06:16] Ethan Park: significant; if prompts share common prefixes or you have template emails / manifest schemas, prefix/KV caching can reduce repeat computation by 30-60% depending on reuse. we'll instrument that in the bench.
[06:30] Priya Singh: timeline — you mentioned 6 weeks, can you break that out?
[06:35] Maya Chen: proposed: week 0: SOW sign, data & security exchange; week 1: ingest and label golden prompts; week 2: bench infra prep and smoke; week 3: baseline bench run (hosted); week 4: iterate on prompt tweaks and regression runs; week 5: run dedicated config tests (if chosen) and finalize metrics; week 6: deliver report and go/no-go.
[06:58] Carlos Mendoza: sounds tight but doable. we may need a 1-week buffer for governance approvals.
[07:05] Ethan Park: totally fine — we can shift the bench window.
[07:10] Priya Singh: on scoring, do you output a report we can attach to execs?
[07:14] Nina Alvarez: yes, final report includes per-case pass rates, hallucination examples, latency/cost breakdown, deployment recommendations and a golden-set failure matrix.
[07:25] Carlos Mendoza: i want to ensure we capture false positives on hallucination detection — detection shouldn't overflag correct but novel outputs.
[07:33] Ethan Park: we tune thresholds on your regression set and review with your SMEs. during the POC one of the activities is to calibrate thresholds using labeled fallback examples.
[07:44] Liam O'Connor: do you do canary or A/B tests? we may want to route 10% traffic to the POC model to see real-world behavior.
[07:52] Maya Chen: yes, Redwood supports canary and gradual rollouts with fallback policies. for POC we can simulate traffic or, if you prefer, do split routing for a short window. A/B will need infra flags on your side.
[08:06] Priya Singh: what's the benchmark environment — are you using gpus in-host or cpu for some tests?
[08:13] Ethan Park: inference is GPU-based for the models we recommend; bench will run on our hosted infra that mirrors Dedicated sizing. we'll include the exact instance types in the SOW, and we can also run a private on-prem bench if you want to evaluate air-gapped.
[08:30] Carlos Mendoza: can we request a reproducible runner? our infra team wants scripts to replay the bench.
[08:36] Ethan Park: yes, we'll deliver a containerized benchmark runner and an IaC script — Terraform & k6 load profiles — and a runbook. we'll also provide tokenization and kv cache knobs in the runner.
[08:55] Sofia Reyes: about golden prompts, do you accept multi-turn history? some cases include prior messages.
[09:00] Ethan Park: yes include full context. in CSV mark context vs instruction; we prefer separate columns for context and query. also mark which pieces are allowed to be referenced from client data to avoid hallucination false positives.
[09:16] Carlos Mendoza: fallback — if the model doesn't meet latency we will want a simpler rules fallback. are there built-in fallbacks?
[09:24] Maya Chen: you can configure fallback policies: lower-capacity model, cached answers, or service degrade to synchronous rules. Redwood supports automatic fallback and circuit-breaker policies.
[09:34] Priya Singh: ok. can you share an example of hallucination examples you flag?
[09:39] Ethan Park: sure — in the deck we'll include sample triggers: invented carrier codes, fabricated timestamps, or instructions that call external systems that weren't in the prompt — those get flagged.
[09:52] Carlos Mendoza: on reporting, can you produce per-route dashboards? we have a dozen route types.
[09:58] Nina Alvarez: yes, Console provides per-route per-model dashboards, token breakdowns, and error traces. we can export CSVs for your data warehouse.
[10:09] Priya Singh: what's the acceptance rubric again?
[10:12] Maya Chen: reiterating: >=85% golden pass, hallucination <3% (regression), format compliance >=98%, 95th pct latency <400ms or documented tradeoff with dedicated option. cost delta within projected budget — we'll model that in SOW.
[10:29] Carlos Mendoza: one more on regression: do you support automated regression diffs between model versions?
[10:34] Ethan Park: yes, Redwood Optimize can run pairwise comparisons and highlight regressions by golden examples and aggregate metrics; we'll include that in the POC run.
[10:44] Priya Singh: any legal/procurement items?
[10:48] Maya Chen: standard procurement steps — we'll hand off to contracts after SOW signed. we can start with a mutual NDA addendum if you want.
[10:57] Carlos Mendoza: ok good. let's talk about labeling effort — any tools?
[11:01] Ethan Park: we provide a small labeling UI for golden set if you need it; many customers prefer to label offline and upload CSV.
[11:10] Priya Singh: what's the approach to scoring ambiguous answers? our SME team sometimes mark 50/50.
[11:16] Ethan Park: for ambiguous cases we support soft scoring: partial credit per subfield plus a human adjudication step; those examples are held out of pass rate calc unless adjudicated. we'll document that in the rubric.
[11:30] Sofia Reyes: can you add format regex checks for JSON outputs? we need strict schema enforcement.
[11:36] Ethan Park: yes, we'll run JSON schema validation as part of format compliance and count failures in the report.
[11:44] Carlos Mendoza: i'm worried about tokenization differences between our local preprocessor and your runner.
[11:50] Ethan Park: we include a tokenization sanity check and will run your tokenizer against the runner; any differences are captured and normalized. we'll add that to the runbook.
[12:03] Priya Singh: ok, recap and next steps?
[12:06] Maya Chen: recap: Redwood to send SOW + pricing and benchmark artifacts; Ethan to share runner and templates; Peregrine to deliver golden set and regression corpus and traffic profile; Nina to send SOC2 and security checklist. we'll target first bench week of 2026-02-09 but subject to Peregrine approvals.
[12:25] Carlos Mendoza: agreed. I'll sync with procurement and get back within 5 business days on approvals.
[12:32] Maya Chen: awesome — we'll follow up via email with all links (deck, runner repo, CSV template).
[12:37] Priya Singh: thanks everyone, good call.
[12:41] Maya Chen: thanks, end meeting.
